record.paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
record.original_question: Once a computable version of the intelligence order relation is available, what experimental behavior does it exhibit across different problem spaces, does it correlate with human IQ test scores, and in restricted domains such as classification or sequence prediction does it rank algorithms in a way that agrees with standard performance measures and observed real-world performance?

evidence.quote: c) Experimental evaluation. Once a computable version of the IOR had been defined, one could write a computer program that implements it. One could then experimentally explore its characteristics in a range of different problem spaces. For example, it might be possible to find correlations with IQ test scores when applied to humans, like has been done with the C-Test [HOMC98]. Another possibility would be to consider more limited domains like classification problems or sequence prediction problems and to see whether the relative performance of algorithms according to the IOR agrees with standard performance measures and real world performance.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background. Let $\mathcal{E}$ denote a class of computable reward-summable environments $\mu:(\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{R})^{*}\to[0,1]$ with rewards in $[0,1]$ and bounded total reward, and let $\mathcal{A}$ denote the class of (possibly stochastic) agents $\pi:(\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{O}\times\mathcal{R})^{*}\to\mathcal{A}$. For an agent $\pi$ interacting with an environment $\mu$, let $V^{\pi}_{\mu}\in[0,1]$ denote the expected total discounted reward. Fix a universal prefix Turing machine $U$ and let $K(\mu)$ denote the prefix Kolmogorov complexity of $\mu$. The Legg–Hutter intelligence order relation is the partial preorder on $\mathcal{A}$ defined by
$$\pi_1 \succeq \pi_2 \iff \forall \mu\in\mathcal{E}:\ V^{\pi_1}_{\mu}\ \ge\ V^{\pi_2}_{\mu},$$
and the universal intelligence of $\pi$ is
$$\Upsilon(\pi) = \sum_{\mu\in\mathcal{E}} 2^{-K(\mu)} V^{\pi}_{\mu}.$$
Both $\succeq$ and $\Upsilon$ are uncomputable in general.

Problem. Construct an explicit computable approximation $\widehat{\Upsilon}$ (equivalently a computable surrogate $\widehat{\succeq}$ of the intelligence order relation), e.g. by restricting $\mathcal{E}$ to a time/space-bounded sub-class of computable environments and replacing $K$ with a resource-bounded complexity measure, and then establish the following:

(a) Prove convergence/consistency: as the resource bound tends to infinity, $\widehat{\Upsilon}\to\Upsilon$ pointwise on a meaningful subclass of agents, and characterize the rate of convergence.

(b) Empirically (or via probabilistic analysis on a specified random model of test instances) determine the distribution of $\widehat{\Upsilon}(\pi)$ across natural agent families and problem spaces, and decide whether $\widehat{\Upsilon}$, when applied to models of human subjects on inductive-inference test batteries (such as C-Test–style sequence-completion problems), produces a quantity that is significantly correlated with measured IQ scores.

(c) For the restricted domains of (i) supervised classification with a fixed loss $\ell$ and (ii) deterministic sequence prediction with log-loss, prove or disprove that the ordering induced by $\widehat{\succeq}$ on standard algorithm classes (e.g., $k$-NN, decision trees, SVMs, neural networks; Laplace/Krichevsky–Trofimov/CTW/LZ-based predictors) coincides, up to ties, with the ordering induced by classical risk or per-symbol redundancy on natural benchmark distributions.

State and resolve each of (a), (b), (c).
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of defining a computable approximation of the Legg–Hutter intelligence order relation and experimentally validating it (correlation with human IQ-style tests, agreement with standard performance measures on classification/sequence prediction) remains an open research program. While related work exists on AIXI approximations (e.g., MC-AIXI-CTW), Hernández-Orallo's anytime universal intelligence tests, and the C-Test, no published result establishes the full experimental characterization requested. No definitive resolution was found.

status_evidence.title: Measuring universal intelligence: Towards an anytime intelligence test
status_evidence.snippet: Hernández-Orallo and Dowe propose anytime intelligence tests inspired by the Legg–Hutter measure; experimental validation across problem spaces and correlations with human performance are discussed as ongoing.
status_evidence.claim: Computable approximations to universal intelligence and their empirical evaluation are an active, unfinished line of research.

status_evidence.title: A Monte-Carlo AIXI Approximation
status_evidence.snippet: Veness et al. give a computable approximation (MC-AIXI-CTW) but do not provide a computable intelligence order relation or correlations with IQ.
status_evidence.claim: Existing approximations address agents but not the full experimental program for the intelligence order relation.
